title: Medical Disorders: Anemia, Drugs and Heart Disease

units.title: Maternal Respiratory Adaptations & Thoracic Anatomy
units.guide: The maternal respiratory system adapts through progesterone-mediated stimulation of the medullary respiratory center, increasing tidal volume by 30-50% while respiratory rate remains constant. Diaphragmatic elevation of 4 cm and subcostal widening decrease functional residual capacity by 20%, while chronic hyperventilation creates a compensated respiratory alkalosis facilitating fetal CO2 transfer.

units.title: Maternal Oxygen Dynamics, Endocrine & Visceral Changes
units.guide: Total maternal oxygen consumption and binding capacity increase alongside a narrower arteriovenous oxygen gradient. The anterior pituitary gland enlarges by 135% with heightened vascularity, rendering it susceptible to ischemic necrosis (Sheehan syndrome) during postpartum hemorrhage. Fetal skeletal demands absorb 30 g of maternal calcium via enhanced active intestinal absorption.

units.title: Iron Requirements, Metabolism & Anemia Mukt Bharat / I-NIPI
units.sec: Iron physiology and national programs · p359-360
units.guide: Total pregnancy iron requirement is 1000 mg (fetal/placental demands 300 mg, RBC expansion 500 mg, basal losses 200 mg), rising to 7.5 mg/day in the third trimester. Because anemia affects 50% of Indian mothers, the Anemia Mukt Bharat (I-NIPI 6x6x6) initiative distributes daily red IFA tablets (60 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid) paired with mid-trimester albendazole deworming.

units.title: IFA Supplementation Rules & Anemia Definitions
units.sec: IFA rules and severity grading · p360-361
units.guide: IFA tablets should be consumed 2 hours post-prandially with water or citrus juices, maintaining a 2-hour separation from calcium or tea to maximize absorption. WHO classifies anemia as <11 g/dL (Mild: 10-10.9, Moderate: 7-9.9, Severe: <7 g/dL), while ICMR designates <4.0 g/dL as very severe anemia. Nutritional iron deficiency accounts for 80% of pathological anemia.

units.title: Maternal & Fetal Complications of Anemia in Pregnancy
units.guide: Severe maternal anemia impairs myometrial oxygenation leading to uterine inertia, postpartum hemorrhage, subinvolution, and heart failure (peaking immediately postpartum due to autotransfusion). While active placental transport shields the fetus from developing microcytic anemia, maternal hypoxemia triggers compensatory placentomegaly, preterm labor, and fetal growth restriction.

units.title: Clinical Evaluation & Physical Workup of Gestational Anemia
units.guide: Clinical history evaluates pica, menorrhagia, and worm infestation; physical examination inspects the conjunctiva, tongue, and palmar creases (pallor evident when Hb <7 g/dL). Severe deficiency produces platonychia, koilonychia (spoon nails), or angular cheilosis. Government guidelines mandate checking hemoglobin at all four routine antenatal visits.

units.title: Diagnostic RBC Indices & Iron Profile Interpretation
units.sec: Laboratory indices and iron panel · p363-364
units.guide: Peripheral blood smear demonstrates microcytic hypochromic red cells in iron deficiency anemia (MCV <75-80 fL, MCHC <30%). The Mentzer index (MCV/RBC count) cleanly differentiates IDA (>13) from beta-thalassemia trait (<13). Serum ferritin (<20-30 mcg/L) serves as the gold-standard biochemical marker of depleted iron stores, accompanied by elevated TIBC (>400 mcg/dL) and transferrin saturation <16%.

units.title: Oral Iron Therapy & Assessing Treatment Response
units.guide: Treatment of mild-to-moderate anemia initiates with 2 IFA tablets daily (120 mg elemental iron). Therapeutic response is verified earliest by a reticulocyte surge within 5-7 days (peaking at 10 days), followed by a hemoglobin rise of 0.7-1.0 g/dL per month. Dark stools confirm medication compliance, and treatment continues until target hemoglobin is reached.

units.title: Parenteral Iron Therapy, Ganzoni Formula & Blood Transfusion
units.guide: Parenteral iron (IV iron sucrose, max 200 mg/day; ferric carboxymaltose) is indicated for oral intolerance, malabsorption, or moderate anemia diagnosed beyond 30-34 weeks. Total deficit is calculated via the Ganzoni equation: Weight x (11 - Hb) x 2.4 + 500 mg. Packed red blood cell transfusion is reserved for acute hemorrhage, heart failure, Hb <5 g/dL at any gestation, or severe anemia near term.

units.title: Trimester-Wise Gestational Management Protocol for Anemia
units.guide: Anemia algorithms integrate gestational age and severity: before 34 weeks, mild-to-moderate anemia receives oral iron; beyond 34 weeks, moderate cases switch to parenteral iron to secure rapid replenishment. Severe anemia (<7 g/dL) near term warrants blood transfusion with furosemide diuresis, while extreme anemia (<5 g/dL) mandates immediate transfusion regardless of gestational age.

units.title: Antimicrobial Safety & Teratogenic Hazards in Pregnancy
units.guide: Penicillins and cephalosporins remain safe throughout gestation, while nitrofurantoin serves as first-line therapy for asymptomatic bacteriuria. Tetracyclines (bone hypoplasia, permanent enamel discoloration), aminoglycosides (eighth cranial nerve ototoxicity), chloramphenicol (Gray baby syndrome), and fluoroquinolones (fetal arthropathy) are strictly avoided.

units.title: Anticoagulation: LMWH, Warfarin & Mechanical Valves
units.guide: Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) does not cross the placental barrier and serves as the anticoagulant of choice throughout gestation, monitored by anti-Factor Xa levels. Warfarin crosses the placenta, causing embryopathy and fetal intracranial hemorrhage. In women with mechanical prosthetic heart valves, warfarin <5 mg/day may be continued in early pregnancy or switched sequentially to LMWH/UFH prior to labor.

units.title: Warfarin Embryopathy (DiSaia Syndrome) & Antiepileptics
units.guide: Warfarin exposure at 6-9 weeks produces DiSaia syndrome, featuring nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses (chondrodysplasia punctata), microcephaly, and optic atrophy. Among antiepileptics, valproate is the most potent teratogen (neural tube and cardiac defects); levetiracetam and lamotrigine display the safest clinical profiles, always co-prescribed with high-dose folic acid.

units.title: Maternal Cardiovascular Hemodynamics & Peak Stress Periods
units.guide: Maternal cardiac output surges by 40-50% while systemic vascular resistance declines, producing a mid-trimester blood pressure nadir. Peak cardiovascular decompensation risks concentrate at 28-32 weeks, during the second stage of labor, and immediately postpartum due to autotransfusion of 300-500 mL of blood from the contracted uterus.

units.title: Heart Failure vs Pregnancy Signs, RHD & Congenital Lesions
units.guide: Physiological systolic flow murmurs (grade <=2/6) and an S3 gallop are benign in pregnancy, whereas any diastolic murmur, systolic murmur >=grade 3/6, or elevated JVP signifies structural heart disease. Rheumatic heart disease with mitral stenosis (MS) is the leading cause of maternal cardiac mortality in developing nations; atrial septal defect represents the most common acyanotic congenital lesion.

units.title: Lesion Prognosis & WHO Class IV Contraindications
units.guide: Stenotic valvular lesions (MS, AS) poorly tolerate gestational tachycardia due to shortened diastolic filling times, precipitating pulmonary edema. Regurgitant lesions (MR, AR) improve due to reduced peripheral vascular resistance. Modified WHO Class IV conditions (Eisenmenger syndrome, severe pulmonary hypertension, severe MS, LVEF <30%, Marfan with aortic root >=45 mm) carry extreme maternal mortality (30-50%), contraindicating pregnancy.

units.title: Intrapartum & Postpartum Management of Heart Disease
units.guide: Vaginal delivery in a semi-recumbent left-lateral position with early epidural analgesia is preferred for cardiac patients, using vacuum or forceps to shorten second-stage pushing. Fluid infusion is restricted to 75 mL/hr. In the third stage, slow IV oxytocin is the agent of choice; methylergometrine is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED because severe vasoconstriction triggers fatal pulmonary edema.

units.title: Peripartum Cardiomyopathy & Mitral Stenosis Management
units.guide: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) presents with heart failure (LVEF <45%) between 36 weeks and 5 months postpartum without prior cardiac disease, managed with diuretics, beta-blockers, and bromocriptine. Severe mitral stenosis (mitral valve area <1.5 cm^2) requires heart rate control with beta-blockers and diuretics, with percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy performed in the second trimester if medical therapy fails.

questions.q: Which maternal lung volume or capacity exhibits a prominent 30% to 50% increase during normal singleton pregnancy?
opts: Tidal volume (VT)
Residual volume (RV)
Functional residual capacity (FRC)
Expiratory reserve volume (ERV)
questions.exp: Progesterone directly stimulates the medullary respiratory center to increase tidal volume by 30-50% (and minute ventilation by 40%). (Book p358)

questions.q: What happens to the maternal respiratory rate (breaths per minute) during normal pregnancy?
opts: It remains essentially constant (or shows a negligible increase)
It doubles from 14 to 28 breaths per minute
It decreases significantly by 40%
It exhibits severe Cheyne-Stokes breathing
questions.exp: The respiratory rate remains unchanged (or shows minimal increase); hyperventilation is achieved via increased tidal volume, not tachypnea. (Book p358)

questions.q: Due to upward displacement of the diaphragm by 4 cm by the enlarging uterus, which lung parameters DECREASE by approximately 20%?
opts: Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) and Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV)
Vital Capacity and Inspiratory Capacity
Tidal Volume and Minute Ventilation
Total Lung Capacity and Anatomical Dead Space
questions.exp: Elevated diaphragm position reduces Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) and Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) by ~20%. (Book p358)

questions.q: What physiological acid-base state is characteristically observed on maternal arterial blood gas analysis during normal pregnancy?
opts: Chronic compensated respiratory alkalosis (pCO2 28-32 mmHg, HCO3 18-22 mEq/L, pH 7.40-7.45)
Uncompensated metabolic acidosis
Severe acute respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia
questions.exp: Progesterone-induced hyperventilation blows off CO2 (pCO2 28-32 mmHg), compensated by renal bicarbonate wasting to maintain arterial pH 7.40-7.45. (Book p358)

questions.q: What is the biological advantage of maternal physiological respiratory alkalosis (low maternal pCO2 of 28-32 mmHg) for the fetus?
opts: It establishes a favorable partial pressure gradient promoting rapid transfer of CO2 from fetal blood into maternal blood
It stimulates fetal renal surfactant synthesis
It prevents premature rupture of fetal membranes
It inhibits fetal cardiac output
questions.exp: Low maternal pCO2 creates a transplacental concentration gradient that facilitates the diffusion of CO2 from the fetal circulation to maternal blood. (Book p358)

questions.q: Fill up: In pregnancy, tidal volume increases by about ______%, which lowers maternal arterial PCO2 to roughly ______ mmHg.
questions.exp: Progesterone-driven hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 to about 30-32 mmHg, creating the gradient for fetal carbon dioxide transfer. (Book p358)

questions.q: During pregnancy, maternal oxygen consumption increases by 20%, but the arteriovenous (A-V) oxygen gradient decreases. Why?
opts: The disproportionate 40-50% surge in maternal cardiac output delivers oxygen far in excess of tissue extraction
Fetal tissue consumes zero oxygen
Maternal hemoglobin cannot bind oxygen
Maternal systemic vascular resistance increases
questions.exp: Because cardiac output increases by 40-50% while O2 consumption increases by only 20%, uterine and systemic A-V O2 differences narrow. (Book p358)

questions.q: During normal pregnancy, the maternal pituitary gland enlarges by approximately 135%, primarily due to hypertrophy of prolactin-secreting lactotrophs. If severe postpartum hemorrhage occurs, this enlarged gland is prone to ischemic necrosis known as:
opts: Sheehan syndrome
Simmonds disease
Nelson syndrome
Schmidt syndrome
questions.exp: Enlargement of the anterior pituitary makes it vulnerable to ischemic infarction during severe hypotension in PPH (Sheehan syndrome). (Book p358)

questions.q: Approximately how much total elemental calcium does the developing fetal skeleton accumulate across pregnancy, and how does maternal physiology supply this?
opts: Approximately 30 g; supplied by doubled maternal intestinal calcium absorption under active 1,25-(OH)2 Vitamin D
Approximately 500 g; supplied by maternal bone resorption
Approximately 5 g; supplied by passive renal retention
Approximately 100 g; supplied by amniotic fluid ingestion
questions.exp: The fetus acquires ~30 g of calcium (mostly in T3), met by doubling maternal intestinal absorption stimulated by 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. (Book p358)

questions.sec: Maternal oxygen dynamics, endocrine & visceral changes
questions.q: Which of the following statements about respiratory physiology in pregnancy is TRUE?
opts: The fall in maternal PaCO2 is what allows fetal carbon dioxide to diffuse into maternal blood
Maternal arterial PO2 falls markedly because oxygen consumption outstrips the rise in ventilation
The gravid uterus pushes the diaphragm downwards, increasing the antero-posterior chest diameter
Functional residual capacity rises during pregnancy, giving the mother more oxygen reserve
questions.exp: PaO2 is normal or slightly higher, the diaphragm rises (transverse diameter widens) and FRC falls, so the pregnant woman desaturates faster. (Book p358)

questions.q: What is the total cumulative elemental iron requirement throughout a normal singleton pregnancy?
opts: About 1000 mg: 300 mg for the fetus and placenta, 500 mg for red cell expansion and 200 mg excreted
About 300 mg: 100 mg for the fetus and placenta, 150 mg for red cell expansion and 50 mg excreted
About 2500 mg: 1000 mg for the fetus and placenta, 1200 mg for red cell expansion and 300 mg excreted
About 500 mg: 200 mg for the fetus and placenta, 250 mg for red cell expansion and 50 mg excreted
questions.exp: The total extra requirement is about 1000 mg of elemental iron, and the breakdown matters when explaining why supplementation is needed. (Book p359)

questions.q: How does iron transfer across the placenta from the maternal circulation into fetal blood?
opts: Active transport via transferrin receptors against a concentration gradient
Simple passive diffusion through intercellular clefts
Facilitated diffusion via GLUT transporters
Pinocytosis of intact maternal erythrocytes
questions.exp: Placental syncytiotrophoblasts extract iron via transferrin receptors and actively pump it to the fetus against a concentration gradient. (Book p359)

questions.q: What is the daily elemental iron requirement during the third trimester of pregnancy?
opts: 7.5 mg/day, compared with about 0.8 mg/day in the first trimester
1.0 mg/day, compared with about 0.8 mg/day in the first trimester
25 mg/day, compared with about 7.5 mg/day in the first trimester
0.5 mg/day, compared with about 7.5 mg/day in the first trimester
questions.exp: Elemental iron needs rise steeply to about 7.5 mg/day in the third trimester, largely for the expanding red cell mass. (Book p359)

questions.q: Under the Anemia Mukt Bharat (I-NIPI) programme, what deworming regimen is routinely administered to pregnant women?
opts: Albendazole 400 mg single oral dose in the second trimester (after 14 weeks)
Albendazole 400 mg daily for 7 days in the first trimester
Mebendazole 100 mg weekly throughout pregnancy
Deworming is contraindicated throughout pregnancy
questions.exp: Under Anemia Mukt Bharat, a single prophylactic dose of Albendazole 400 mg is administered during the 2nd trimester to treat hookworm infestation. (Book p359)

questions.sec: Iron requirements, metabolism & Anemia Mukt Bharat / I-NIPI
questions.q: Fill up: The total extra iron requirement of a pregnancy is about ______ mg, of which roughly ______ mg goes to the fetus and placenta.
questions.exp: About 1000 mg extra iron is needed in total: the largest share expands the maternal red cell mass and about 300 mg goes to the fetus and placenta. (Book p359)

questions.q: What are the two active pharmacological ingredients in the prophylactic RED IFA tablet distributed under the national programme?
opts: 60 mg elemental iron (as ferrous sulfate) and 500 mcg folic acid
100 mg elemental iron and 1 mg folic acid
30 mg elemental iron and 400 mcg folic acid
200 mg elemental iron and 5 mg folic acid
questions.exp: Each red IFA tablet contains 60 mg elemental iron (dried ferrous sulfate) and 500 mcg folic acid. (Book p360)

questions.q: When is the optimal time for a pregnant woman to consume her daily oral iron tablet to maximize bioavailability and reduce GI discomfort?
opts: 2 hours after meals (or at bedtime), avoiding co-ingestion with tea, milk, or calcium tablets
Immediately before breakfast with a large cup of milk
Simultaneously with calcium carbonate tablets
With hot black tea to stimulate gastric acidity
questions.exp: Iron is best absorbed on an empty stomach or 2 hours post-meal; tannins in tea and calcium in milk inhibit iron absorption. (Book p360)

questions.q: Fill up: Anaemia in pregnancy is diagnosed when the haemoglobin is below ______ g/dL, and severe anaemia when it is below ______ g/dL.
questions.exp: WHO defines anaemia in pregnancy as haemoglobin below 11 g/dL, with severe anaemia below 7 g/dL and moderate between 7 and 9.9 g/dL. (Book p360)

questions.q: According to World Health Organization (WHO) criteria, what hemoglobin cutoffs define mild, moderate, and severe anemia in pregnancy?
opts: Mild: 10.0 to 10.9 g/dL; Moderate: 7.0 to 9.9 g/dL; Severe: < 7.0 g/dL
Mild: 11.0 to 11.9 g/dL; Moderate: 9.0 to 10.9 g/dL; Severe: < 9.0 g/dL
Mild: 9.0 to 10.0 g/dL; Moderate: 6.0 to 8.9 g/dL; Severe: < 6.0 g/dL
Mild: 10.5 to 11.0 g/dL; Moderate: 8.0 to 10.4 g/dL; Severe: < 8.0 g/dL
questions.exp: WHO defines anemia in pregnancy as Hb <11.0 g/dL (Mild: 10-10.9; Moderate: 7-9.9; Severe: <7.0 g/dL; ICMR adds Very severe: <4.0 g/dL). (Book p361)

questions.q: What is the single most common pathological cause of anemia in pregnant women worldwide?
opts: Nutritional iron deficiency anemia (IDA, ~80% of cases)
Megaloblastic folate deficiency
Beta-thalassemia major
Aplastic anemia
questions.exp: Nutritional iron deficiency anemia accounts for approximately 80% of all pathological anemias encountered in pregnancy. (Book p361)

questions.q: Why does maternal severe anemia stimulate compensatory placentomegaly (abnormally large placenta)?
opts: To increase the villous surface area in an attempt to compensate for decreased maternal oxygen-carrying capacity
Due to excessive deposition of fetal fat in the cotyledons
Because iron accumulates within chorionic villi
Secondary to cytomegalovirus infection
questions.exp: In severe maternal anemia, chronic hypoxemia stimulates placental hypertrophy and capillary branching, causing placentomegaly. (Book p361)

questions.sec: Maternal & fetal complications of anemia in pregnancy
questions.q: All of the following are recognised consequences of severe maternal anaemia EXCEPT:
opts: Fetal macrosomia
Preterm labour and low birth weight
High-output cardiac failure
Postpartum haemorrhage from poor myometrial contractility
questions.exp: Severe anaemia impairs oxygen transfer and myometrial function, so growth restriction and preterm birth occur; macrosomia does not. (Book p361)

questions.q: Why are severely anemic women at exceptionally high risk of developing postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) immediately following placental delivery?
opts: Myometrial tissue hypoxia impairs smooth muscle contractility, resulting in severe uterine atony
Anemia causes disseminated intravascular coagulation in all patients
Anemia causes rapid cervical lacerations
Platelets cannot aggregate in anemic blood
questions.exp: Severe tissue hypoxia prevents the living ligatures (interlacing myometrial fibers) from contracting effectively, precipitating atonic PPH. (Book p362)

questions.q: At what specific time point during childbirth is an anemic woman at the greatest risk of acute congestive heart failure and pulmonary edema?
opts: Immediately postpartum, following placental delivery and uterine contraction
During the latent phase of the first stage of labor
At 20 weeks of gestation
During early lactation 2 weeks postpartum
questions.exp: Immediately postpartum, uterine contraction autotransfuses 300-500 mL of blood into the systemic circulation, acutely overloading the compromised heart. (Book p362)

questions.q: Does moderate maternal iron deficiency anemia typically cause microcytic hypochromic anemia in the neonate at birth?
opts: No, because the placenta actively extracts iron against a gradient, maintaining normal neonatal hemoglobin at the expense of maternal stores
Yes, the fetus always reflects the exact maternal hemoglobin concentration
Yes, fetal hemoglobin drops to zero
Only if the infant is male
questions.exp: The placenta actively transports iron, preserving normal fetal/neonatal hemoglobin; however, neonatal iron stores are depleted. (Book p362)

questions.q: A pregnant woman presents with an intense craving to eat non-food substances such as dirt, clay, raw rice, or ice. This symptom is known as:
opts: Pica, a classic clinical manifestation of severe iron deficiency
Bulimia nervosa, with repeated bingeing and purging behaviour
Hyperemesis gravidarum, with protracted vomiting and ketosis
Chorea gravidarum, with involuntary movements of the limbs
questions.exp: Craving and chewing non-food substances such as clay, raw rice or ice is pica, and it accompanies severe iron deficiency. (Book p362)

questions.sec: Clinical evaluation & physical workup of gestational anemia
questions.q: A 26-year-old at 30 weeks has a haemoglobin of 8.2 g/dL with pallor, koilonychia, a smooth sore tongue and pica. Which single investigation best confirms the underlying diagnosis?
opts: Serum ferritin estimation
Serum vitamin B12 assay
Haemoglobin electrophoresis
Direct Coombs test
questions.exp: Koilonychia, glossitis and pica point to iron deficiency, and serum ferritin is the most specific single test of iron stores. (Book p362)

questions.q: On physical examination of a pregnant female, clinical pallor becomes distinctly evident on inspection of the palmar creases when the hemoglobin level drops below:
questions.exp: Pallor of the palmar creases is a reliable clinical sign indicating severe anemia with hemoglobin < 7.0 g/dL. (Book p363)

questions.q: Koilonychia—spoon-shaped concave nails with raised edges—is a specific physical sign indicative of:
opts: Chronic, severe iron deficiency anemia
Folate deficiency megaloblastic anemia
Hemolytic jaundice
Sickle cell disease
questions.exp: Koilonychia (spooning of nails) and platonychia (flat nails) are pathognomonic physical signs of chronic tissue iron depletion. (Book p363)

questions.q: According to Government of India (MOHFW) guidelines, how frequently should hemoglobin be screened during antenatal care?
opts: At every routine antenatal visit (4 times during pregnancy)
Only once at the booking visit
Only in the third trimester at 36 weeks
Only if the patient appears visibly pale
questions.exp: In India, MOHFW mandates checking hemoglobin at each of the 4 routine antenatal visits to detect and manage progressive anemia. (Book p363)

questions.q: What is the Mentzer Index formula, and what cutoffs differentiate Iron Deficiency Anemia from Beta-Thalassemia Trait?
opts: Mentzer Index = MCV / RBC count; > 13 favors Iron Deficiency Anemia, < 13 favors Beta-Thalassemia Trait
Mentzer Index = Hb / MCV; > 20 favors IDA, < 20 favors Thalassemia
Mentzer Index = MCHC / Ferritin; > 5 favors IDA
Mentzer Index = Hematocrit / WBC; > 10 favors Thalassemia
questions.exp: Mentzer index = MCV (fL) / RBC count (millions/mcL). In IDA, RBC count is low, giving index >13; in thalassemia trait, RBC count is high, giving index <13. (Book p364)

questions.q: What is considered the gold-standard, most sensitive non-invasive biochemical test to confirm depleted iron stores and diagnose Iron Deficiency Anemia?
opts: Serum Ferritin (< 20 to 30 mcg/L)
Serum Iron alone
Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) alone
Peripheral blood smear alone
questions.exp: Serum ferritin <20-30 mcg/L is the single best, earliest, and most sensitive biochemical marker of iron deficiency (normal 20-200 mcg/L). (Book p364)

questions.q: In a patient with classical Iron Deficiency Anemia, what typical pattern of iron study parameters is expected?
opts: Decreased serum iron (<40 mcg/dL), elevated TIBC (>400 mcg/dL), and decreased transferrin saturation (<16%)
Elevated serum iron, decreased TIBC, and elevated ferritin
Normal iron, normal TIBC, and elevated transferrin saturation
Decreased serum iron and decreased TIBC
questions.exp: IDA is characterized by low serum ferritin, low serum iron (<40 mcg/dL), elevated TIBC (>400 mcg/dL), and transferrin saturation <10-16%. (Book p364)

questions.q: How does Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) differ between Iron Deficiency Anemia and Anemia of Chronic Disease?
opts: TIBC is elevated in Iron Deficiency Anemia, but decreased/normal in Anemia of Chronic Disease
TIBC is decreased in IDA, but elevated in chronic disease
TIBC is identical and zero in both conditions
TIBC is elevated in both conditions
questions.exp: In IDA, transferrin synthesis rises, producing high TIBC (>400 mcg/dL); in chronic disease/inflammation, hepcidin and cytokines reduce TIBC. (Book p364)

questions.sec: Diagnostic RBC indices & iron profile interpretation
questions.q: Match the laboratory pattern with the diagnosis — 1) Microcytic hypochromic cells with a low ferritin 2) Macrocytic cells with hypersegmented neutrophils 3) Microcytosis with a normal ferritin and a raised HbA2 … A) Beta thalassaemia trait B) Iron deficiency anaemia C) Folate or vitamin B12 deficiency
questions.exp: Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency, macrocytosis with hypersegmented neutrophils means megaloblastosis, and a raised HbA2 with normal iron means thalassaemia trait. (Book p364)

questions.q: When initiating oral therapeutic iron for anemia in pregnancy, what is the standard recommended daily dose of IFA tablets?
opts: 2 IFA tablets per day (delivering 120 mg of elemental iron)
1 IFA tablet every alternate day
4 IFA tablets per day with meals
1 IFA tablet per week
questions.exp: Therapeutic oral iron therapy requires 2 IFA tablets daily (total 120 mg elemental iron) until target hemoglobin is achieved. (Book p365)

questions.q: What is the EARLIEST objective hematological marker indicating an adequate therapeutic response to oral iron therapy?
opts: An increase in reticulocyte count within 5 to 7 days (peaking at 10 days)
An increase in hemoglobin concentration within 24 hours
A drop in serum ferritin within 3 days
A sudden decrease in total iron binding capacity
questions.exp: A reticulocyte surge beginning at 5-7 days and peaking at 10 days is the earliest and preferred proof of therapeutic bone marrow response. (Book p365)

questions.q: A pregnant woman taking oral iron therapy has a repeat hemoglobin checked after 1 month. What rise in hemoglobin defines an 'adequate' response?
opts: A rise of >= 1.0 g/dL after 1 month of therapy
A rise of >= 4.0 g/dL after 1 month
A rise of 0.1 g/dL after 1 month
No change in hemoglobin is required
questions.exp: An adequate response is defined as an increase in hemoglobin of >=1.0 g/dL after 3-4 weeks of compliant oral iron therapy. (Book p365)

questions.q: What is the most common reason for failure of oral iron therapy in a pregnant patient, and how can the clinician objectively verify adherence?
opts: Non-compliance from gastrointestinal side effects, which blackening of the stool can confirm
Severe intestinal malabsorption, demonstrated by a negative stool test
Bone marrow aplasia, which should always be excluded by aspiration
Excessive urinary excretion of iron, measured in a 24-hour collection
questions.exp: The commonest reason is that she has stopped taking it because of nausea or constipation; asking about black stools is a simple objective check. (Book p365)

questions.sec: Oral iron therapy & assessing treatment response
questions.q: Fill up: An adequate response to oral iron is a haemoglobin rise of about ______ g/dL over ______ weeks.
questions.exp: A rise of roughly 1 g/dL in 3-4 weeks confirms adherence and absorption; failure prompts a search for malabsorption or non-iron causes. (Book p365)

questions.q: Which of the following is a recognized clinical indication for administering parenteral (intravenous) iron therapy in pregnancy?
opts: Severe gastrointestinal intolerance or non-compliance to oral iron, or moderate anemia diagnosed late in gestation (>30-34 weeks)
Mild anemia diagnosed at 8 weeks of gestation
Patient preference for intravenous injections in the first trimester
Hemochromatosis
questions.exp: Parenteral iron is indicated for oral intolerance, non-compliance, malabsorption, or moderate anemia presenting beyond 30-34 weeks. (Book p366)

questions.q: What is the Ganzoni formula used to calculate total elemental iron deficit for parenteral iron therapy?
opts: Total deficit (mg) = [Body weight (kg) x (Target Hb 11 - Actual Hb) x 2.4] + 500 mg (iron stores)
Total deficit (mg) = Body weight x Actual Hb x 10
Total deficit (mg) = Gestational age x (11 - Hb) x 100
Total deficit (mg) = [Height (cm) x Hb] + 1000 mg
questions.exp: Ganzoni formula: Iron deficit (mg) = [Weight in kg x (Target Hb 11 - Patient's Hb) x 2.4] + 500 mg for storage replenishment. (Book p366)

questions.q: What is the maximum single daily dose and weekly ceiling for intravenous iron sucrose administration in pregnancy?
opts: Up to 200 mg per day diluted and infused over 15-30 minutes, and up to 600 mg per week
Up to 1000 mg per day diluted and infused over 15-30 minutes, with no weekly ceiling
Up to 50 mg per day diluted and infused over 15-30 minutes, and up to 200 mg per week
Up to 200 mg per day diluted and infused over 15-30 minutes, and up to 2000 mg per week
questions.exp: Iron sucrose is given in divided doses: a maximum of 200 mg per day infused over 15-30 minutes and 600 mg per week. (Book p366)

questions.q: One unit of packed red blood cells (PRBC) typically elevates the maternal hemoglobin concentration by approximately:
opts: About 1.0 g/dL, and the haematocrit by about three percentage points
About 0.2 g/dL, and the haematocrit by about one percentage point
About 3.0 g/dL, and the haematocrit by about nine percentage points
About 5.0 g/dL, and the haematocrit by about fifteen percentage points
questions.exp: A rough rule is that one unit of packed cells raises the haemoglobin by about 1 g/dL and the haematocrit by about 3 per cent. (Book p366)

questions.sec: Parenteral iron therapy, Ganzoni formula & blood transfusion
questions.q: Which of the following statements about parenteral iron in pregnancy is TRUE?
opts: Iron sucrose is the preferred parenteral preparation; iron dextran needs a test dose because of anaphylaxis risk
Intramuscular iron into the gluteal region is the preferred parenteral route in the third trimester
Total-dose iron infusion is the treatment of choice in the first trimester for severe anaemia
Parenteral iron must never be given once the haemoglobin has fallen below 7 g/dL
questions.exp: Iron sucrose and ferric carboxymaltose are safe after the first trimester; iron dextran risks anaphylaxis, and intramuscular iron is painful and stains the skin. (Book p366)

questions.q: A pregnant woman presents at 28 weeks of gestation with moderate anemia (Hb 8.5 g/dL). What is the appropriate initial management protocol?
opts: Oral iron therapy (2 IFA tablets daily) with repeat hemoglobin assessment after 3-4 weeks
Immediate blood transfusion of 2 units of packed RBCs
Immediate parenteral iron sucrose infusion
Emergency induction of labor
questions.exp: At <34 weeks with mild-to-moderate anemia, oral iron (2 tablets/day) is first line; parenteral iron is reserved for failures or late presentation. (Book p367)

questions.q: A pregnant woman is first diagnosed with moderate anemia (Hb 8.0 g/dL) at 35 weeks of gestation. Why is parenteral iron preferred over oral iron?
opts: Parenteral iron replenishes iron stores rapidly before delivery, whereas oral iron takes 4-6 weeks to achieve adequate hemoglobin rise
Oral iron is contraindicated after 34 weeks of gestation
Parenteral iron induces spontaneous cervical ripening
Parenteral iron crosses the placenta faster
questions.exp: At >=34 weeks, delivery is imminent; parenteral iron rapidly delivers the calculated deficit, whereas oral iron is too slow. (Book p367)

questions.q: A pregnant woman presents at 24 weeks of gestation with very severe, symptomatic anemia and a hemoglobin of 4.2 g/dL (< 5 g/dL). What is the immediate treatment of choice?
opts: Packed red blood cell transfusion accompanied by IV furosemide, irrespective of gestational age
Double-dose oral iron therapy for 1 month
Intravenous iron sucrose 200 mg daily
Immediate termination of pregnancy
questions.exp: A hemoglobin < 5.0 g/dL at ANY gestational age is a critical medical emergency carrying high risk of heart failure, dictating PRBC transfusion. (Book p367)

questions.sec: Trimester-wise gestational management protocol for anemia
questions.q: A primigravida at 14 weeks has a haemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL with breathlessness on climbing one flight of stairs. What is the most appropriate plan?
opts: Admit, start parenteral iron sucrose, continue oral iron to term and recheck the haemoglobin in four weeks
Transfuse packed cells immediately and deliver the pregnancy whatever the gestation
Continue oral iron alone and review the haemoglobin at 28 weeks
Recommend termination because severe anaemia before viability is unmanageable
questions.exp: In the second trimester a symptomatic woman with severe anaemia needs parenteral iron; transfusion is reserved for decompensation or an imminent need for delivery. (Book p367)

questions.q: Which of the following antibiotic classes is considered SAFE and serves as first-line therapy across all trimesters of pregnancy?
opts: Penicillins (e.g., Ampicillin, Amoxicillin) and Cephalosporins
Fluoroquinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin)
Tetracyclines (e.g., Doxycycline)
Aminoglycosides (e.g., Gentamicin)
questions.exp: Beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins and cephalosporins) do not interfere with fetal development and are safe throughout gestation. (Book p368)

questions.q: Why are tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline) strictly contraindicated after the 15th week of gestation?
opts: They chelate with calcium in fetal bones and teeth, causing permanent yellowish-brown discoloration, enamel hypoplasia, and bone growth inhibition
They cause Gray baby syndrome
They cause congenital deafness due to 8th cranial nerve damage
They trigger fetal aplastic anemia
questions.exp: Tetracyclines deposit in mineralizing fetal bone and tooth deciduous buds, causing permanent teeth staining and impaired bone growth. (Book p368)

questions.q: What fetal adverse effect is specifically associated with maternal aminoglycoside (streptomycin, gentamicin) use during pregnancy?
opts: Cranial nerve VIII damage leading to permanent sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular ototoxicity
Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus
Phocomelia and amelia
Epstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve
questions.exp: Aminoglycosides cross the placenta and accumulate in fetal endolymph, damaging the 8th cranial nerve and causing congenital deafness. (Book p368)

questions.q: Why is the administration of sulfonamides (e.g., sulfamethoxazole) contraindicated during the late third trimester near delivery?
opts: They displace bilirubin from albumin binding sites, precipitating neonatal kernicterus
They induce maternal gestational diabetes
They cause Gray baby syndrome
They trigger fetal limb reduction defects
questions.exp: Near term, sulfonamides compete for albumin binding sites, displacing unconjugated bilirubin into neonatal brain tissue and causing kernicterus. (Book p368)

questions.sec: Antimicrobial safety & teratogenic hazards in pregnancy
questions.q: All of the following antimicrobials are regarded as safe in pregnancy EXCEPT:
opts: Tetracyclines
Penicillins
Cephalosporins
Macrolides such as erythromycin
questions.exp: Tetracyclines stain fetal teeth and bones and are avoided; penicillins, cephalosporins and macrolides are safe in pregnancy. (Book p368)

questions.q: Why is Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH, Enoxaparin) the anticoagulant of choice throughout pregnancy?
opts: Because its large molecular weight and negative charge prevent it from crossing the placental syncytiotrophoblast barrier
Because it is an oral tablet with zero maternal bleeding risk
Because it permanently reverses prosthetic valve thrombosis
Because it accelerates fetal lung maturity
questions.exp: Heparins (both LMWH and UFH) do not cross the placenta and are neither teratogenic nor cause fetal hemorrhage. (Book p368)

questions.q: What laboratory assay is standardly utilized to monitor the therapeutic efficacy and dosing of Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH)?
opts: Anti-Factor Xa assay (therapeutic target 0.8 to 1.2 IU/mL for mechanical valves)
International Normalized Ratio (INR)
Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT)
Bleeding Time (BT)
questions.exp: LMWH does not predictably prolong the aPTT; it is monitored using peak anti-Factor Xa levels (0.8-1.2 IU/mL for prosthetic valves). (Book p368)

questions.q: At what gestational age is the teratogenic risk of maternal Warfarin exposure at its absolute peak?
opts: First trimester between 6 and 9 weeks of gestation
Second trimester between 18 and 22 weeks
Third trimester at 36 weeks
Immediately during active labor
questions.exp: Warfarin teratogenicity is maximal between 6 and 9 weeks (critical window for nasal cartilage and epiphyseal development). (Book p368)

questions.q: A pregnant woman with a mechanical heart valve taking therapeutic Warfarin unexpectedly enters active labor at 37 weeks. What is the mandatory management?
opts: Stop warfarin, perform Caesarean delivery, and administer Vitamin K to both mother and neonate to avoid fetal intracranial hemorrhage
Allow spontaneous vaginal delivery with vacuum extraction
Administer high-dose intravenous aspirin
Discharge the patient until warfarin washes out
questions.exp: Vaginal delivery while anticoagulated with warfarin risks fatal fetal intracranial trauma; Caesarean section with Vitamin K is mandatory. (Book p369)

questions.q: Match the exposure with its fetal consequence — 1) Warfarin between 6 and 12 weeks 2) Warfarin near term and in labour 3) Low molecular weight heparin … A) Does not cross the placenta and is the preferred agent B) Warfarin embryopathy with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses C) Fetal and neonatal intracranial haemorrhage during delivery
questions.exp: Warfarin teratogenicity peaks in organogenesis, near-term use risks fetal bleeding, and heparin molecules do not cross the placenta. (Book p369)

questions.q: DiSaia syndrome (Fetal Warfarin Syndrome), caused by early first-trimester coumarin exposure, is characterized by which classic triad?
opts: Hypoplasia of the nasal bridge, stippled epiphyses and central nervous system abnormalities
Phocomelia, amelia and ano-rectal atresia in the affected infant
Ebstein anomaly, fetal goitre and bilateral renal agenesis
Cleft lip, cleft palate and postaxial polydactyly
questions.exp: DiSaia syndrome is warfarin embryopathy: nasal hypoplasia, chondrodysplasia punctata and central nervous system defects. (Book p369)

questions.q: Which antiepileptic medication carries the HIGHEST risk of major congenital malformations (including neural tube defects, craniofacial, and cardiac anomalies)?
opts: Valproic acid (Sodium valproate)
Levetiracetam
Lamotrigine
Carbamazepine
questions.exp: Valproate is the most teratogenic antiepileptic (10% major malformation rate, including NTDs and developmental delay). (Book p369)

questions.q: If a woman with epilepsy conceives while on antiepileptic therapy, what is the recommended clinical management strategy?
opts: Continue the same drug at the lowest effective dose as monotherapy, and prescribe high-dose folic acid (4 to 5 mg/day)
Immediately stop all antiepileptic drugs to prevent birth defects
Switch her to multiple high-dose antiepileptics
Terminate the pregnancy unconditionally
questions.exp: Abrupt drug withdrawal triggers status epilepticus (fatal to fetus); maintain seizure control with lowest effective monotherapy + high-dose folic acid. (Book p369)

questions.q: Fill up: The critical window for warfarin embryopathy is between ______ and ______ weeks of gestation.
questions.exp: Exposure from 6 to 12 weeks produces nasal hypoplasia and chondrodysplasia punctata; later exposure mainly risks central nervous system and bleeding problems. (Book p369)

questions.q: By how much does maternal cardiac output physiologically increase during normal singleton pregnancy, and when does this rise peak antenatally?
opts: Increases by 40% to 50%, reaching its antenatal peak at 28 to 32 weeks of gestation
Increases by 10%, peaking at 12 weeks
Increases by 100%, peaking at 40 weeks
Decreases by 20% in the third trimester
questions.exp: Cardiac output rises by 40-50% (driven by stroke volume early, heart rate late), peaking antenatally at 28-32 weeks. (Book p370)

questions.q: During normal pregnancy, maternal systemic blood pressure drops to its nadir during which period, and what physiological mechanism is responsible?
opts: Mid-second trimester (20-24 weeks); driven by progesterone- and nitric oxide-mediated systemic vasodilation lowering peripheral vascular resistance
First trimester at 6 weeks; driven by maternal dehydration
Third trimester at 38 weeks; driven by placental ischemia
Blood pressure never changes during normal pregnancy
questions.exp: Systemic vascular resistance falls due to progesterone, relaxin, and nitric oxide, producing a blood pressure nadir at 20-24 weeks. (Book p370)

questions.q: Which of the following cardiovascular physical findings is considered entirely PHYSIOLOGICAL during normal pregnancy and does not signify heart disease?
opts: Grade 1-2/6 mid-systolic ejection murmur heard best at the left sternal border
Any diastolic murmur
Loud, prominent S4 gallop
Continuous machinery murmur over the left infraclavicular area
questions.exp: A functional ejection systolic murmur (grade <=2/6) over the pulmonary area and an S3 are normal in >90% of pregnant women due to hyperdynamic flow. (Book p370)

questions.q: What normal anatomical displacement of the heart occurs on chest X-ray and ECG during the third trimester as the uterus elevates the diaphragm?
opts: The heart is displaced upward and laterally to the left, producing mild apparent cardiomegaly and left-axis deviation on ECG
The heart is pushed downward into the abdomen
The cardiac apex rotates to the right hemithorax (dextrocardia)
The heart becomes completely obscured by pleural effusion
questions.exp: Diaphragmatic elevation pushes the apex beat to the 4th intercostal space lateral to the midclavicular line, simulating cardiomegaly and left axis shift. (Book p370)

questions.sec: Maternal cardiovascular hemodynamics & peak stress periods
questions.q: Fill up: Maternal cardiac output rises by about ______% in pregnancy and peaks around ______ weeks.
questions.exp: Output rises early and peaks at 20-24 weeks; further surges occur during labour and immediately after delivery. (Book p370)

questions.q: Which of the following physical signs or symptoms in a pregnant woman is unequivocally PATHOLOGICAL and diagnostic of organic cardiac disease?
opts: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, hemoptysis, diastolic murmur, and persistent Jugular Venous Pressure > 8 cm H2O
Mild dependent ankle edema subsiding after night rest
Mild breathlessness when climbing two flights of stairs
Resting heart rate increase of 10-15 bpm
questions.exp: Diastolic murmurs, hemoptysis, orthopnea, PND, clubbing, and elevated JVP (>8 cm H2O) are pathological signs of structural cardiac disease. (Book p371)

questions.q: What is the most common cause of heart disease in pregnancy in developing countries like India, and which specific valvular lesion is most frequently encountered?
opts: Rheumatic Heart Disease (70-80%); Mitral Stenosis (80-90%)
Congenital Heart Disease; Coarctation of the aorta
Ischemic coronary heart disease; Myocardial infarction
Peripartum cardiomyopathy; Dilated cardiomyopathy
questions.exp: Rheumatic heart disease accounts for the majority of maternal cardiac disease in developing nations, with mitral stenosis being the classic predominant lesion. (Book p371)

questions.q: What is the most common acyanotic congenital heart disease encountered in pregnant women?
opts: Atrial Septal Defect (ASD, ostium secundum type)
Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)
Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)
Coarctation of the aorta
questions.exp: Secundum ASD is the most common congenital cardiac lesion seen in adult pregnancy, generally well tolerated unless pulmonary hypertension develops. (Book p371)

questions.q: What is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease encountered in pregnant women?
opts: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)
Transposition of the great arteries (TGA)
Tricuspid atresia
Ebstein anomaly
questions.exp: Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic heart defect; uncorrected TOF carries high maternal mortality and fetal loss rates. (Book p371)

questions.sec: Heart failure vs pregnancy signs, RHD & congenital lesions
questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes pathological heart disease from the normal cardiovascular changes of pregnancy?
opts: A loud P2, a third heart sound and persistent basal crepitations are pathological, while a soft systolic flow murmur is not
Exertional dyspnoea in a pregnant woman is always pathological and needs echocardiography
Any systolic murmur heard over the pulmonary area in pregnancy indicates organic valve disease
Pedal oedema in the third trimester always indicates incipient cardiac failure
questions.exp: Breathlessness, a soft ejection murmur and ankle oedema are common in normal pregnancy; a loud P2, gallop rhythm and persistent crepitations are not. (Book p371)

questions.q: Why do stenotic cardiac lesions (e.g., Mitral Stenosis, Aortic Stenosis) decompensate severely during pregnancy, whereas regurgitant lesions (Mitral Regurgitation) often improve?
opts: Tachycardia shortens diastolic filling in stenosis, while low resistance helps regurgitant lesions
Progesterone dilates stenotic valves and worsens the pressure gradient
Oestrogen closes regurgitant valves completely during pregnancy
Stenotic lesions are unaffected by the blood volume shifts of pregnancy
questions.exp: Stenotic lesions cannot increase output through a fixed orifice and tachycardia shortens filling; regurgitant lesions benefit from the fall in resistance. (Book p371)

questions.q: Under the modified WHO classification of maternal cardiovascular risk, what is the defining feature of WHO Class IV conditions?
opts: Pregnancy is strictly CONTRAINDICATED; maternal mortality is extremely high (up to 30-50%), and termination is advised if conception occurs
Pregnancy is completely safe with routine outpatient visits
Caesarean delivery must be performed at 28 weeks
Only oral iron therapy is needed
questions.exp: mWHO Class IV carries prohibited risk of maternal mortality (up to 30-50%); pregnancy is contraindicated, and termination is recommended if pregnant. (Book p371)

questions.q: Which of the following maternal cardiac conditions is classified under WHO Class IV, carrying the HIGHEST risk of maternal mortality (30-50%)?
opts: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension / Eisenmenger syndrome
Repaired uncomplicated ventricular septal defect
Mild asymptomatic mitral regurgitation
Small patent ductus arteriosus
questions.exp: Eisenmenger syndrome and severe pulmonary arterial hypertension carry a catastrophic 30-50% maternal mortality, primarily peripartum. (Book p371)

questions.q: A pregnant woman with Marfan syndrome undergoes echocardiographic evaluation of her ascending aorta. At what aortic root diameter is pregnancy strictly contraindicated or termination strongly advised?
opts: Aortic root diameter >= 40 to 45 mm (due to high risk of fatal aortic dissection or rupture)
Aortic root diameter >= 20 mm
Aortic root diameter >= 30 mm
Aortic root diameter is irrelevant in Marfan syndrome
questions.exp: An aortic root diameter >=40-45 mm in Marfan syndrome carries an extreme risk of lethal aortic dissection or rupture during pregnancy and labor. (Book p371)

questions.sec: Lesion prognosis & WHO class IV contraindications
questions.q: All of the following are WHO class IV lesions in which pregnancy is contraindicated EXCEPT:
opts: Mild mitral stenosis in NYHA class I
Pulmonary arterial hypertension of any cause
Severe left ventricular dysfunction with an ejection fraction below 30%
Severe mitral stenosis with severe pulmonary hypertension
questions.exp: Mild mitral stenosis with good functional class is a class II lesion with a small risk; the others carry prohibitive maternal mortality. (Book p371)

questions.q: In a pregnant woman with stable, compensated cardiac disease, what is the preferred mode of delivery?
opts: Spontaneous or induced vaginal delivery, as Caesarean section entails greater blood loss, infection risk, and hemodynamic instability
Routine elective Caesarean section under general anesthesia at 34 weeks
Emergency vacuum extraction at 32 weeks
Home birth with water immersion
questions.exp: Vaginal delivery is preferred for cardiac patients because Caesarean delivery produces twice the blood loss and dramatic hemodynamic shifts. (Book p372)

questions.q: Why is an instrumental delivery (vacuum or low forceps) routinely planned to assist the second stage of labor in a patient with cardiac disease?
opts: To cut short and eliminate strenuous maternal bearing-down efforts (Valsalva maneuvers), which produce sharp cardiac workload swings
To prevent fetal macrosomia
Because cardiac drugs cause complete uterine paralysis
Because cardiac patients cannot feel labor contractions
questions.exp: Elective assistance with forceps or vacuum avoids prolonged maternal pushing and Valsalva efforts, protecting the heart from acute preload surges. (Book p372)

questions.q: During the active management of the third stage of labor in a woman with heart disease, what is the drug of choice for uterotonic prophylaxis, and what drug is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED?
opts: Slow IV oxytocin infusion is the drug of choice; Methylergometrine is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED
Methylergometrine is the drug of choice; Oxytocin is contraindicated
Carboprost is the drug of choice; Misoprostol is contraindicated
Ergometrine and oxytocin should be given simultaneously in high doses
questions.exp: Oxytocin infusion is the drug of choice. Methylergometrine is contraindicated because it induces sustained vasoconstriction, hypertension, and pulmonary edema. (Book p372)

questions.q: What intravenous fluid rate restriction is recommended during intrapartum care of a woman with cardiac disease to avoid volume overload?
opts: Restrict total IV fluids to <= 75 mL/hour
Rapid bolus of 500 mL/hour normal saline
Total fluid restriction to 0 mL/hour
Continuous infusion of 250 mL/hour dextrose
questions.exp: IV fluids are restricted to <=75 mL/hr to prevent iatrogenic circulatory overload and flash pulmonary edema in cardiac mothers. (Book p372)

questions.sec: Intrapartum & postpartum management of heart disease
questions.q: A primigravida with tight mitral stenosis reaches full cervical dilatation. Which intrapartum measure matters most for her safety?
opts: Cut the second stage short with forceps or vacuum under epidural analgesia and avoid Valsalva pushing
Encourage a long second stage of spontaneous pushing to avoid any instrumentation
Give intramuscular ergometrine with the delivery of the anterior shoulder
Withhold analgesia so that warning symptoms of failure are not masked
questions.exp: Epidural analgesia and instrumental shortening of the second stage blunt the dangerous cardiac output surges, and ergometrine is avoided. (Book p372)

questions.q: What clinical criteria define Peripartum Cardiomyopathy (PPCM)?
opts: Heart failure from left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction below 45% in the last month or first five months postpartum
Spontaneous coronary artery dissection presenting at 20 weeks of gestation
Aortic valve vegetations appearing during the first year after delivery
A congenital ventricular septal defect first detected in the third trimester
questions.exp: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is defined by its timing, by systolic dysfunction and by the absence of another identifiable cause. (Book p373)

questions.q: In addition to standard heart failure pharmacotherapy, which novel drug targeting the 16-kDa prolactin cleavage fragment has shown therapeutic benefit in Peripartum Cardiomyopathy?
opts: Bromocriptine (dopamine agonist that inhibits pituitary prolactin release)
Oxytocin antagonist (Atosiban)
Mifepristone
Carbergoline in high doses for lactation induction
questions.exp: 16-kDa prolactin promotes endothelial apoptosis in PPCM; bromocriptine blocks prolactin release and improves myocardial recovery. (Book p373)

questions.q: Match the lesion with its description — 1) Peripartum cardiomyopathy 2) Mitral stenosis 3) Severe aortic stenosis … A) Systolic dysfunction appearing in the last month of pregnancy or the first five months after delivery B) Diastolic murmur with a loud first sound and opening snap; tachycardia is poorly tolerated C) Fixed cardiac output, so obstruction makes labour and delivery extremely dangerous
questions.exp: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is defined by its timing, mitral stenosis is a diastolic lesion that cannot raise output through tachycardia, and aortic stenosis fixes output. (Book p373)

questions.q: In a pregnant woman with moderate-to-severe Mitral Stenosis (valve area < 1.5 cm^2), what is the first-line medical therapy to prevent pulmonary edema?
opts: Beta-blockers (e.g., Metoprolol) to control heart rate and prolong diastolic ventricular filling time
High-dose intravenous hydralazine to induce tachycardia
Digoxin monotherapy to increase heart rate
Atropine bolus to maintain pulse > 120 bpm
questions.exp: Beta-blockers slow the heart rate, prolonging diastolic filling across the narrowed mitral valve and lowering left atrial pressure to prevent pulmonary edema. (Book p374)

questions.q: When medical therapy fails in a pregnant patient with severe, refractory symptomatic Mitral Stenosis, what surgical/interventional procedure is preferred, and in which trimester?
opts: Percutaneous Transvenous Mitral Commissurotomy (PTMC / Balloon Valvotomy), ideally performed in the second trimester
Open cardiopulmonary bypass valve replacement in the first trimester
Emergency mechanical valve replacement during active labor
Transapical aortic valve implantation at 12 weeks
questions.exp: PTMC (balloon mitral valvotomy) is the intervention of choice for refractory severe MS, ideally performed in the 2nd trimester after organogenesis. (Book p374)
